title: Early Christianity: First Century to Constantine
subtitle: How a movement's growth bears on the authority of its beliefs
summary: Christianity's earliest sources already center Jesus's death and resurrection; devotion to his divinity did not begin with Constantine. Later expansion, debate, persecution, and imperial support shaped the Church, but neither growth nor doctrinal development by itself proves or disproves revelation. Islam's alternative must be supported by its own prophetic claim.

seo.metaTitle: Early Christianity: First Century to Constantine | The Straight Path
seo.metaDescription: From early Christian proclamation to Nicaea: what growth, suffering, and doctrinal development do—and do not—establish about religious authority.

sections.title: From a Movement to a Claim of Authority
sections.body:
Islam calls people to honor Jesus while worshiping the one God, and presents the Quran as guidance that corrects later religious claims. This alternative requires a positive case, developed in [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran); a history of Christian disagreements alone cannot establish it.

The distinct historical question is how the beliefs and institutions of a growing movement relate to Jesus's authority. Early testimony, later clarification, and political success are relevant, but they are not the same kind of evidence.

sections.title: The Cross Was Not a Late Imperial Invention
sections.body:
The Christian proclamation of Jesus's death appears in Paul's early testimony, including 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, and in the Gospel narratives. Mainstream historians regard crucifixion under Pilate as well established. It cannot plausibly be attributed to Constantine's fourth-century intervention.

Quran 4:157 gives the mainstream Islamic reading a real disagreement with that conclusion. Quran 3:55 presents God's raising of Jesus. [The Historical Jesus](/articles/the-historical-jesus) addresses the evidential difficulty without dismissing the Christian sources as worthless.

sections.title: Resurrection Belief Was Already Central
sections.body:
In 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, Paul says he transmitted a received tradition about death, burial, resurrection, and appearances. Luke 24:1–6 and Acts 1:3 also present the risen Jesus as central to the movement's identity.

These sources establish that resurrection was not an explanation invented centuries later to support an emperor's church. Whether the experiences and testimony establish the resurrection itself is a further question. Historical evidence can bear on it; merely observing that the witnesses believed does not complete the argument.

sections.title: The Jerusalem Community Matters
sections.body:
Acts 2:22–24 portrays Peter proclaiming Jesus's death and resurrection in Jerusalem. Acts 2:1–4 describes the community in terms of the Spirit's activity. These are the author's theological accounts, but they are important evidence for the movement's understanding of its origin.

Jesus's followers were not simply absent while Paul invented a replacement religion. Paul's own reports of contact with Jerusalem leaders, discussed in [Paul and His Influence](/articles/paul-and-his-influence), prevent that oversimplification. Agreement, conflict, and competing accounts all require careful interpretation.

sections.title: Expansion Raised Real Questions
sections.body:
A movement rooted in Israel had to address the standing of non-Jewish believers, the place of Jewish practice, and the meaning of allegiance to Jesus. Paul was an influential participant in those debates, not their only actor.

Romans 1:1–4 frames his message through Israel's scriptures and Jesus's identity. Matthew 28:18–20 presents a mission to the nations. Christian expansion therefore cannot be reduced either to an obvious betrayal of Judaism or to a development that requires no argument for its continuity.

sections.title: Suffering Shows Commitment, Not Infallibility
sections.body:
Early Christian writing includes costly commitment, conflict, and persecution. [Ignatius's letter to the Smyrnaeans](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0109.htm) links suffering, bodily resurrection, and devotion to Jesus. [Tacitus, Annals 15.44](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/tacitus-annals/15-44), is an outside Roman witness to Christians' punishment under Nero, not an eyewitness account of Jesus's ministry.

Such evidence makes dismissal of all early Christians as cynical inventors implausible. Sincerity and courage deserve recognition, but do not make every belief infallible. That distinction applies equally to other religious movements.

sections.title: From Legal Protection to Nicaea
sections.body:
The policy associated with Constantine and Licinius in 313 granted religious liberty and restored Christian property; [Lactantius, chapter 48](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0705.htm), preserves its language. This was not yet the establishment of Christianity as the empire's sole official religion.

Constantine later convened Nicaea in 325 to address an existing church dispute. Nicaea did not invent all belief in Jesus's divinity or choose the Bible's books. [The council's separate study](/articles/council-of-nicaea) examines what its authority could establish.

sections.title: An Objection: Does Development Imply Corruption?
sections.body:
No. A Christian can argue that new questions require clearer language without changing the original truth. That possibility must be allowed. Every religious community also interprets, teaches, and systematizes its sources; Islam is not exempt from those activities.

The issue is whether a particular development preserves the source's meaning and has legitimate authority to bind worship. Neither the presence of councils nor the absence of a finished technical formula in an earlier text settles that by itself. Evidence and interpretation must be examined together.

sections.title: The Islamic Difference Is Not Merely Institutional
sections.body:
Quran 2:87 honors Jesus as a messenger supported by signs. In Quran 5:117, Jesus's testimony directs worship to God. Islam makes that Creator-messenger distinction the governing principle of devotion.

The invitation is not to admire a less organized religion or to assume that later means false. It is to examine whether the Quran's account of God and prophethood is true. If it is revelation, it has authority beyond an institution's success; if that is not established, institutional development alone cannot prove Islam.

sections.title: History That Leads to a Real Question
sections.body:
The useful next step is to separate three claims: what early Christians proclaimed, whether the proclamation is well supported, and whether later institutions had authority to define it. [The Historical Jesus](/articles/the-historical-jesus), [Paul and His Influence](/articles/paul-and-his-influence), and [The Council of Nicaea](/articles/council-of-nicaea) pursue those different questions.

The lived issue remains worship and trust. Historical inquiry should make that decision better informed, not turn people from either tradition into caricatures.

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا
quranVerses.translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَىٰٓ إِنِّى مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَىَّ وَمُطَهِّرُكَ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ وَجَاعِلُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوكَ فَوْقَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَأَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ فِيمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ
quranVerses.translation: [Mention] when Allah said, "O Jesus, indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve and make those who follow you [in submission to Allah alone] superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: مَا قُلْتُ لَهُمْ إِلَّا مَآ أَمَرْتَنِى بِهِۦٓ أَنِ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّى وَرَبَّكُمْ ۚ وَكُنتُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًۭا مَّا دُمْتُ فِيهِمْ ۖ فَلَمَّا تَوَفَّيْتَنِى كُنتَ أَنتَ ٱلرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ وَأَنتَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ شَهِيدٌ
quranVerses.translation: I said not to them except what You commanded me - to worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Observer over them, and You are, over all things, Witness.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَلَقَدْ ءَاتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَقَفَّيْنَا مِنۢ بَعْدِهِۦ بِٱلرُّسُلِ ۖ وَءَاتَيْنَا عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ وَأَيَّدْنَٰهُ بِرُوحِ ٱلْقُدُسِ ۗ أَفَكُلَّمَا جَآءَكُمْ رَسُولٌۢ بِمَا لَا تَهْوَىٰٓ أَنفُسُكُمُ ٱسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ فَفَرِيقًۭا كَذَّبْتُمْ وَفَرِيقًۭا تَقْتُلُونَ
quranVerses.translation: And We did certainly give Moses the Torah and followed up after him with messengers. And We gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the Pure Spirit. But is it [not] that every time a messenger came to you, [O Children of Israel], with what your souls did not desire, you were arrogant? And a party [of messengers] you denied and another party you killed.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.

“Men of Israel, hear these words! Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him among you, even as you yourselves know, him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed; whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it.

But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb. They entered in, and didn’t find the Lord Jesus’ body. While they were greatly perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling clothing. Becoming terrified, they bowed their faces down to the earth. They said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee,
To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom.

Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Good News of God, which he promised before through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was born of the offspring of David according to the flesh, who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,

Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place. Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.

Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.

faq.question: Did Constantine invent belief in Jesus's divinity?
faq.answer: No. Earlier Christian texts already give Jesus divine status. Constantine's involvement changed the political setting of doctrinal decisions, not the existence of all earlier devotion.

faq.question: Did legalization in 313 make Christianity the empire's sole official religion?
faq.answer: No. The policy preserved by Lactantius granted religious liberty and restored property. Legal protection and sole official establishment are different.

faq.question: Does persecution prove a movement's beliefs true?
faq.answer: No. It can show costly commitment and deserves moral seriousness, but sincerity is not the same as infallibility.

faq.question: Does doctrinal development automatically prove corruption?
faq.answer: No. Development can be clarification or change. Its relation to the sources and its claim to bind belief require examination.

furtherReading.title: The Historical Jesus: A Comprehensive Guide
furtherReading.author: Gerd Theissen and Annette Merz
furtherReading.note: A comprehensive scholarly overview of Jesus and early Christianity that integrates historical-critical methods with systematic theological reflection. Fortress Press, 1998. Accessible while maintaining academic rigor.

furtherReading.title: The Apostolic Fathers: Greek Texts and English Translations
furtherReading.author: Michael W. Holmes (translator and editor)
furtherReading.note: Authoritative bilingual edition of the Apostolic Fathers (Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, Didache, and others) with Greek texts and English translations. Baker Academic, 3rd ed., 2007. Primary sources that illuminate early church life, theology, and responses to persecution.

furtherReading.title: The Cambridge Ancient History Vol. XI: The High Empire, A.D. 70-192
furtherReading.author: Edited by Alan K. Bowman, Peter Garnsey, Dominic Rathbone
furtherReading.note: Includes chapters on early Christianity within its broader Roman historical context, balancing Christian sources with external historical evidence.

furtherReading.title: Jesus and the Victory of God
furtherReading.author: N.T. Wright
furtherReading.note: Wright's study of the historical Jesus within first-century Judaism, including Jesus' proclamation, messianic vocation, and movement toward the cross.
